title: The Teddy Bear
subtitle: Mississippi, November 1902
intro: A president refused a shot he thought unsporting. A cartoonist drew it. A Brooklyn shopkeeper wrote for permission to use the name. Twelve questions on how a hunting trip in the Mississippi Delta produced the most successful toy in the world — and on the man who actually caught the bear.
heroAlt: Clifford Berryman's cartoon "Drawing the line in Mississippi"
heroCredit: "Drawing the line in Mississippi," Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

badge.title: The Teddy Bear
badge.shareText: I scored {score}/{total} on the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library's Teddy Bear quiz — {tier}. Try it:

tiers.name: Holt Collier
tiers.line: Perfect. Nobody knows this country better.

tiers.name: Toymaker
tiers.line: You know how it was made.

questions.prompt: Where was the 1902 hunt that produced the teddy bear?
options: The Mississippi Delta, near Smedes
The Louisiana canebrakes
The Ozarks in Arkansas
The Great Smoky Mountains
questions.explanation: Deep in the Mississippi Delta near the village of Smedes, on land between the Mississippi River and the Little Sunflower. Roosevelt arrived on a Thursday afternoon in November 1902 with rain glazing the rails and storm clouds coming, and declared himself ready to hunt.
questions.imageAlt: Berryman's cartoon of Roosevelt refusing to shoot the bear
questions.credit: "Drawing the line in Mississippi," Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Who led the hunt as Roosevelt's guide?
options: Roosevelt hunted without a guide
Holt Collier, a Mississippi bear hunter
A party of Delta planters who knew the country
Ben Lilly, the celebrated Louisiana houndsman
questions.explanation: Holt Collier, then fifty-six, chosen because no one in the Delta could track a bear like him. He had been born into slavery in 1846, killed his first bear with a twelve-gauge Scott shotgun in a swamp at the age of ten, ran away at fourteen and — improbably, and to Roosevelt's fascination — served with the Confederate army before coming home to the Delta to hunt. He had guided for more than thirty years by 1902 and is credited with taking some three thousand bears in his lifetime, a figure that says as much about the century as about the man. Ben Lilly was a real Roosevelt guide, but on a different hunt: the Louisiana canebrakes in 1907.
questions.imageAlt: Berryman's 1902 cartoon of the Mississippi bear hunt
questions.credit: "Drawing the line in Mississippi," Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What happened when the hunting party finally cornered a bear?
options: It broke through the dogs and escaped into the canebrake
It was found dead, killed by the dogs
It was caught alive and tied up
Roosevelt brought it down with a single clean shot
questions.explanation: The dogs brought it to bay and it was roped and secured so the president could have his shot — the whole point of the expedition being that the president should get a bear. In the struggle the bear seized one of Collier's dogs and killed it. By the time Roosevelt rode up to the spot the animal was exhausted, injured and tied fast, and the hunt everyone had planned for months had arranged itself into something he wanted no part of.
questions.imageAlt: A later Berryman cartoon featuring the bear
questions.credit: "To the Woods!" Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What was the bear tied to?
options: A stake driven in the mud
A fence post
A wagon wheel
A willow tree
questions.explanation: A willow. Roosevelt afterwards described it as a poor, ragged thing the hunting guides had tied to a willow tree — which tells you what he thought of the arrangement.
questions.imageAlt: Berryman's cartoon of the tied bear
questions.credit: "Drawing the line in Mississippi," Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Why did Roosevelt refuse to shoot it?
options: He had run out of ammunition
He was too far away for a clean shot
He judged it unsportsmanlike
He had already filled his quota
questions.explanation: Shooting a tethered animal was not hunting, and he would not do it. This was a man who had spent twenty years writing about the ethics of the chase; the refusal was entirely in character and no part of it was staged for the press.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt turning away from the tied bear in Berryman's cartoon
questions.credit: "Drawing the line in Mississippi," Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

options: It was cut loose and released unharmed
It was killed anyway
It was crated and sent to a zoo in Washington
It broke free in the night and escaped
questions.explanation: This is the part the toy leaves out. The animal was exhausted, injured and beyond saving, and Roosevelt ordered it put out of its misery — he simply would not be the one to claim it as a trophy. The refusal was about sportsmanship, not mercy, and the cartoon that followed quietly turned the one into the other. Nothing in the story ends with a bear walking free into the canebrake.
questions.imageAlt: A later Berryman cartoon featuring the bear
questions.credit: "To the Woods!" Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Who drew the cartoon that made the story famous?
options: Clifford Berryman
Joseph Keppler
Thomas Nast
Homer Davenport
questions.explanation: Clifford K. Berryman, whose drawing ran on the front page of the next day's Washington Post. He titled it "The Passing Show," but almost nobody calls it that — it is remembered by its caption instead.
questions.credit: "Drawing the line in Mississippi," Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

options: The President's Mercy
Teddy's Bear
A Square Deal for the Bear
Drawing the Line in Mississippi
questions.explanation: "Drawing the Line in Mississippi." Many scholars read the caption as a double meaning — the line Roosevelt drew at shooting a tied bear, and a second line being drawn in Mississippi over race. The cartoon is funnier and sharper than the toy it produced.
questions.credit: "Drawing the line in Mississippi," Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: How did the bear in Berryman's drawings change as he kept reusing it?
options: It grew larger and fiercer with each drawing
It shrank into a small cub
It vanished from his cartoons within a year
It stayed exactly as he first drew it
questions.explanation: The animal in the first drawing is a full-grown bear. Berryman kept it in cartoon after cartoon for the rest of his career and it dwindled with each appearance, ending as the small, round-eyed, wide-mouthed cub everybody now pictures. Toy makers copied the cartoon rather than the hunt — which is why the teddy bear is cute and the real one was not.
questions.imageAlt: The shrunken cartoon bear in a later Berryman drawing
questions.credit: "To the Woods!" Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Who made the first American toy bears inspired by the cartoon?
options: F.A.O. Schwarz, the New York toy emporium
Margarete Steiff in Germany
Rose and Morris Michtom
The Milton Bradley company of Springfield, Massachusetts
questions.explanation: Rose Michtom, moved by the story, sewed two plush bears stuffed with excelsior and put them in the window of the small Brooklyn shop she and her husband kept. Her husband Morris had the commercial idea that followed, wrote to the White House, and built the whole thing into the Ideal Novelty and Toy Company — which is why the first American teddy bear and the first American teddy bear manufacturer are the same two people.
questions.credit: "To the Woods!" Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What did Morris Michtom do before selling the toy under Roosevelt's name?
options: Sold it under a different name for a year
Nothing — he never asked
Registered a trademark
Wrote to the president asking permission
questions.explanation: He wrote to the White House asking permission to market it as "Teddy's Bear," and Roosevelt granted it. There is a nice irony in that: Roosevelt disliked being called Teddy, and signed away his nickname to a toy that has carried it for more than a century.
questions.imageAlt: Berryman's cartoon that inspired the toy
questions.credit: "Drawing the line in Mississippi," Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Meanwhile in Germany, someone was making stuffed bears entirely independently. Who?
options: Margarete Steiff, a seamstress in Giengen
Nobody — the toy was purely American
The Bing brothers of Nuremberg
Käthe Kruse, the German dollmaker
questions.explanation: Margarete Steiff, who had survived polio and built a soft-toy business in the small town of Giengen. Her nephew Richard sketched brown bears at the Stuttgart and Munich zoos and persuaded her to make one. At first nobody bought them. The two stories met in the American market and the teddy bear became a craze on both sides of the Atlantic.
questions.credit: "To the Woods!" Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.
